feedback: If the child writes '63' with no unit, ask: '63 what? Is 63 cm the same as 63 cm²?' and point to the tiled squares.
If the child writes '63 cm', show that cm measures a length along an edge, while the squares filling the rectangle each cover an area, so the count of squares is cm².
When the child supplies '63 cm²' and explains it counts unit squares, confirm that the unit now carries the meaning of the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Area counts how many unit squares cover a region, so its unit is a square unit (cm²); a bare number says how many but not of what, and a plain length unit (cm) describes a distance, not a covering.
learnerActions: Enter or write the area of a rectangle, e.g. '63'.
Fill (or draw) the rectangle with unit squares that tile it exactly, counting the squares.
Revise the answer to carry a square unit: '63 cm²' or '63 square centimetres'.
Contrast an edge length of 63 cm (a length measured along one side) with an area of 63 cm² (unit squares covering the inside), and say why they are different quantities.
Answer the prompt: 'why does the unit have to be square?'
activities.title: Tiling to find the unit for area

feedback: If the child writes '15:45 pm', ask: 'What does the pm add, or clash with? Does 24-hour time use am/pm?'
If the child cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm, model the subtraction 15 − 12 = 3 and show both naming the same instant.
Confirm success when the child keeps the systems separate and converts between them fluently with a reason.
activities.intendedInsight: 24-hour and 12-hour are two complete, separate ways of naming the same moment; 'pm' belongs only to the 12-hour system, so stamping it onto a 24-hour time mixes two systems and contradicts itself.
learnerActions: Read a time written in 24-hour notation, e.g. 15:45.

Convert it to 12-hour am/pm: for times from 13:00 to 23:59, subtract 12 from the hour and write pm (15 − 12 = 3, giving 3:45 pm); 12:00–12:59 stays 12 and is pm, 00:00–00:59 becomes 12 am, and 01:00–11:59 keep their hour and are am. Check both show the same moment on a dual clock display.
Decide whether '15:45 pm' can be correct, and explain what the 'pm' clashes with.
Write the same time correctly in each system and state that 24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 with no am/pm.
activities.title: One moment, two clocks: 24-hour vs am/pm

feedback: If the child says 'big angle' or 'small angle', ask them to compare it to a right angle and attach the term acute or obtuse to that comparison.
If acute and obtuse are swapped, re-anchor on the right-angle template: acute is smaller, obtuse is larger.
Confirm when the child names the type and can say how they are sure.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle names are defined by comparison to a right angle (acute < right < obtuse), so the right angle is the reference that makes the vocabulary precise and reliable.
learnerActions: Place or overlay a right-angle template on a given angle.
Decide whether the angle is smaller than a right angle (acute), exactly a right angle (right angle), or larger than a right angle but less than a straight angle (obtuse).
State the angle type using the correct term and justify it by the comparison, avoiding 'big angle' or 'small angle'.
Repeat for several angles, including some close to a right angle.
activities.title: Naming angles against a right angle

feedback: If the child treats 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as different, show both pointing to the same ¾ and the same shaded region.
When the child reads a symbol aloud and explains its meaning, confirm the term and symbol are linked to meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: A value can have more than one correct name; 'quarter' and 'fourth' are two words for the same part, and symbols carry fixed meanings that should be read and explained, not just copied.
learnerActions: Match fraction words to symbols, e.g. 'three quarters' = 'three fourths' = ¾.
Explain that 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' name the same amount, not two different amounts.
Read notation aloud (=, <, >, ÷, ×) and state what each symbol means in a given statement.
activities.title: Two names, one value: fraction vocabulary
